newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia to speed privatisation, new tax code-Chubais.
newsitem.headline: Russia to speed privatisation, new tax code-Chubais.

text.p: Russia's new government is ready to usher in the next stage of economic reform with faster privatisation, a new tax code and property rights, First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais said on Tuesday.

Chubais, who was appointed by President Boris Yeltsin to oversee the economy ten days ago, told Reuters the success of reforms helped the country from sliding into the chaos of Albania and other eastern European nations.
Asked how he would address the most painful problem, that of non-payment of debt by both the government and private sector, he replied:
"For solving that problem first we need property rights, we need to develop the securities market, to speed up the privatisation process and that is something on the agenda of the government."

Chubais, who headed Russia's huge post-Soviet privatisation programme that started in 1992, said the team of reformists now entrusted with helping Russia recover from its economic woes had learned from past mistakes.
"I think that (because of) the experience of the reform process in (the) negative and positive sense we are able now to take the next step, which will bring success," he said, speaking in English.
"The reform in Russia in 1991 and 1992 was unprecedented and nobody anywhere else had such success in the reform process," he added.

"Due to the success of reform Russia is still a country without, let us say, the troubles -- look at Albania, look at Bulgaria one month ago, look at other eastern European countries. Nothing in Russia," he said.

Yeltsin on Monday unveiled a new cabinet with several new reformist faces, including the liberal governor of Nizhny Novgorod, Boris Nemtsov, who will serve alongside Chubais as a first deputy prime minister.
Chubais was also named finance minister in the reshuffle.
He said the government was moving "aggressively" to finish a new large tax code to restructure the country's tortured tax system.
"Now my team and I are very aggressive in finishing this document...the new tax constitution for Russia," he said, adding parts of this document would be submitted soon to parliament.

"There are various options for increasing the tax collection even before the Duma will accept the tax code," he said. "What is necessary is political will. That is something which is in the present government."
As "I am sure we shall be able to demonstrate, it will give good results," he said.

The country's new economy tsar also hailed the other newcomers in the government, calling them the best political team assembled in the country since 1992, and said they are ready to add new energy to reform.
